Calibrating confidence scores

Source: vignettes/calibration.Rmd
calibration.Rmd

This vignette covers the second stage of sheepdog in detail: turning BirdNET confidence scores into probabilities that a detection is a true positive, scoring every detection, and building nightly detection histories. Each step is run on the example data shipped with the package.

library(sheepdog)
library(dplyr)
ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")

Why calibrate

A BirdNET confidence score is a classifier output in [0, 1], not a probability that the detection is correct. The BirdNET authors recommend converting the scores into probabilities of a true detection (Wood & Kahl 2024). One way to do so, with a sample of manually validated detections, is a logistic regression of the verdict on logit(score), applied, for instance, by Owens et al. (2026).

One curve for all species is rarely enough. The same score can mean different things for different species, because the score distributions of true and false detections differ among species, and for the same species at different sites, because the rate of false detections depends on background noise and the rate of true ones on how often the species is present. sheepdog therefore fits hierarchical logistic models in which the intercept and the slope on logit(score) can vary among species and among sites.

The example data

The example data are simulated (data-raw/make_example_data.R). Eight anuran species were recorded at four sites over six months, from October 2021 to March 2022. When a species is present, its true detections have scores drawn from a species-specific Beta distribution. Every species also produces false positives in every recording, present or not, with scores drawn from a second species-specific Beta distribution. For five species (boa_ran, den_nan, lep_fus, pse_pla, sci_nas) the two distributions overlap widely; the other three (ela_bic, lep_pod, phy_cuv) produce few false positives, with low scores, and are well separated. The rate of false positives is multiplied by a site noise factor (ARA 0.7, BAI 1.0, XAR 1.5, NHE 2.2). Presence varies with season and site, including a random preference of each species for each site. The same score therefore corresponds to different probabilities of a true detection among species and sites. The verdicts of the reviewed clips come from the simulated truth.

The reviewed clips are the validation_by_clip_<site>.csv tables written by post_validation(). read_validations() stacks them, keeps the clips with a positive or negative verdict and a confidence score, and adds logit_conf and the binary response tp.

val_files <- list.files(file.path(ex, "validation"), full.names = TRUE)
val <- read_validations(val_files)
#> 2467 reviewed clips (1577 TP / 890 FP) of 8 species at 4 sites.
table(val$site, val$species)
#>      
#>       boa_ran den_nan ela_bic lep_fus lep_pod phy_cuv pse_pla sci_nas
#>   ARA      80      80      80      33      80      80      80      80
#>   BAI      80      80      80      56      58      80      80      80
#>   NHE      80      80      80      80      80      80      80      80
#>   XAR      80      80      80      80      80      80      80      80

The clips were selected with the "top" design (the two highest scores per site x species x night x hour, at most 80 per site x species). Cells where a species was rarely detected hold fewer clips (as few as 33). Precision differs widely among species:

val |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(clips = n(), precision = mean(tp),
            min_conf = min(confidence), median_conf = median(confidence))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   species clips precision min_conf median_conf
#>   <fct>   <int>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 boa_ran   320     0.725    0.101       0.753
#> 2 den_nan   320     0.497    0.108       0.641
#> 3 ela_bic   320     0.894    0.1         0.810
#> 4 lep_fus   249     0.394    0.105       0.490
#> 5 lep_pod   298     0.856    0.104       0.840
#> 6 phy_cuv   320     0.9      0.107       0.845
#> 7 pse_pla   320     0.312    0.106       0.648
#> 8 sci_nas   320     0.497    0.121       0.657

Candidate models

calibration_models() returns the family of candidate models. All of them are binomial regressions of tp on logit_conf. They differ in how the calibration curve is allowed to vary among species and sites.

models <- calibration_models()
cat(paste0(names(models), ": ", vapply(models, deparse1, "")), sep = "\n")
#> m0_global: tp ~ logit_conf
#> m1_species_intercept: tp ~ logit_conf + (1 | species)
#> m2_species_slope: tp ~ logit_conf + (logit_conf | species)
#> m3_plus_site: tp ~ logit_conf + (logit_conf | species) + (1 | site)
#> m4_species_x_site: tp ~ logit_conf + (logit_conf | species) + (1 | site:species)
  • m0_global: one curve for all species and sites (a GLM).
  • m1_species_intercept: species shift the curve along the score axis.
  • m2_species_slope: species also differ in how steeply the probability rises with the score.
  • m3_plus_site: as m2, plus a site intercept shared by all species.
  • m4_species_x_site: as m2, plus an intercept for each site x species combination. This is the most flexible model.

Models m1 to m4 are binomial GLMMs fitted with lme4::glmer().

Comparing models by cross-validation

compare_calibration_models() fits every candidate with k-fold cross-validation and computes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) on the held-out folds. By default, clips are assigned within site x species. The fold assignment uses a fixed seed. Five folds run in a few seconds on these data. Clips from the same recording may then appear on both sides; use grouped folds when evaluating new recordings or nights.

cv <- compare_calibration_models(val, models, k_folds = 5)
#> Cross-validation (5 folds) of 5 models...
cv |> select(model, auc_mean, auc_sd, n_failed)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   model                auc_mean  auc_sd n_failed
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>   <dbl>    <int>
#> 1 m4_species_x_site       0.942 0.00563        0
#> 2 m3_plus_site            0.928 0.00640        0
#> 3 m2_species_slope        0.916 0.00556        0
#> 4 m1_species_intercept    0.902 0.00544        0
#> 5 m0_global               0.862 0.0120         0

The table is ordered by mean AUC. Read the differences between models together with the spread among folds (auc_sd), and check n_failed (folds whose fit failed and were left out of the mean; none here). In the example, each added level of structure raises the mean AUC by more than the fold-to-fold standard deviation: from 0.862 for the global model to 0.902 with species intercepts, 0.916 with species slopes, 0.928 with site intercepts and 0.942 with site x species intercepts. When differences are of the same order as auc_sd, the order of the table can change with k_folds or seed.

AUC measures discrimination (whether true detections score higher than false ones), not calibration (whether a predicted probability of 0.9 is correct nine times in ten). Two models with equal AUC can still give different probabilities, so the comparison is a first filter, not the whole decision.

Scoring the probabilities and choosing a model

The comparison also scores the predicted probabilities themselves on the held-out folds. The log-loss and the Brier score are proper scoring rules: their expected value is best when the predicted probabilities are the true ones, so they reward correct probabilities and not only their ranking (Gneiting & Raftery 2007). The log-loss penalises confident mistakes heavily, which is where p_min operates. The calibration intercept and slope come from a logistic regression of the verdicts on the logit of the predicted probabilities in each test fold: a well calibrated model has intercept 0 and slope 1, and a slope below 1 means probabilities that are too extreme. prop_singular is the share of fold fits that were singular.

cv |>
  select(model, logloss_mean, logloss_sd, brier_mean, cal_intercept,
         cal_slope, prop_singular)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   model logloss_mean logloss_sd brier_mean cal_intercept cal_slope prop_singular
#>   <chr>        <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 m4_s…        0.291    0.0103      0.0941      0.00448      0.993           1  
#> 2 m3_p…        0.317    0.0119      0.104      -0.00268      0.991           0.2
#> 3 m2_s…        0.337    0.0102      0.112      -0.000204     0.987           0.2
#> 4 m1_s…        0.379    0.00934     0.123      -0.00279      0.992           0  
#> 5 m0_g…        0.436    0.0172      0.142      -0.000629     1.00            0

select_calibration_model() applies a selection rule to this table. "best_auc" takes the highest mean AUC, the rule calibrate() uses by default in 2.x. "one_se_logloss" leaves out the models that are singular in most folds and, among the rest, keeps the simplest one whose mean log-loss is within one standard error of the lowest. This is the default in 3.0.0. See vignette("migration-3.0.0") for the migration guide.

select_calibration_model(cv, "best_auc")
#> [1] "m4_species_x_site"
select_calibration_model(cv, "one_se_logloss", k_folds = 5)
#> [1] "m3_plus_site"

Here the highest AUC belongs to m4_species_x_site, singular in 100 % of the folds, and the log-loss rule retains m3_plus_site. calibration_models(uncorrelated = TRUE) adds a sixth candidate, the m4 structure without the correlation between the species intercepts and slopes, which is the term that makes m4 singular (see the next section):

models_u <- calibration_models(uncorrelated = TRUE)
cv_u <- compare_calibration_models(val, models_u, k_folds = 5)
#> Cross-validation (5 folds) of 6 models...
cv_u |> select(model, auc_mean, logloss_mean, logloss_sd, prop_singular)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   model                          auc_mean logloss_mean logloss_sd prop_singular
#>   <chr>                             <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 m4_species_x_site                 0.942        0.291    0.0103            1  
#> 2 m5_species_x_site_uncorrelated    0.941        0.292    0.0112            0  
#> 3 m3_plus_site                      0.928        0.317    0.0119            0.2
#> 4 m2_species_slope                  0.916        0.337    0.0102            0.2
#> 5 m1_species_intercept              0.902        0.379    0.00934           0  
#> 6 m0_global                         0.862        0.436    0.0172            0
select_calibration_model(cv_u, "one_se_logloss", k_folds = 5)
#> [1] "m5_species_x_site_uncorrelated"

calibrate() takes the rule in select and the extra candidate with uncorrelated = TRUE. Whether the retained model is a sound fit is a separate question, taken up next.

Fitting the calibration model

fit_calibration() fits a model to all the reviewed clips and stores the species and site levels with it, for score_detections() and plot_calibration(). We fit every candidate, because whether a GLMM is singular is part of the choice:

fits <- lapply(models, function(f) fit_calibration(val, f))
#> Warning: Singular fit (boundary) of the calibration model tp ~ logit_conf +
#> (logit_conf | species) + (1 | site:species): a variance component is estimated
#> at zero or a correlation at +-1. Check lme4::VarCorr(fit) and consider a
#> simpler model.
vapply(fits[-1], lme4::isSingular, logical(1))
#> m1_species_intercept     m2_species_slope         m3_plus_site 
#>                FALSE                FALSE                FALSE 
#>    m4_species_x_site 
#>                 TRUE
fit_global <- fits$m0_global
fit_full   <- fits$m4_species_x_site
coef(fit_global)
#> (Intercept)  logit_conf 
#>  -0.5310926   1.5993695
lme4::fixef(fit_full)
#> (Intercept)  logit_conf 
#>  -0.2818959   2.8003911
lme4::VarCorr(fit_full)
#>  Groups       Name        Std.Dev. Corr  
#>  site:species (Intercept) 1.19511        
#>  species      (Intercept) 0.81885        
#>               logit_conf  1.89780  1.000

The site x species intercepts of m4 have a standard deviation of 1.2 on the logit scale, a large effect: at a given score, the odds of a true detection differ several-fold among sites for the same species. The fit is nevertheless singular, which is why fit_calibration() warned above (it is the only singular fit among the candidates): the correlation between the species intercepts and slopes is estimated at 1, on the boundary of its range. With 8 species, a correlation between two random effects is poorly identified. A singular fit means that the random-effect structure is more complex than the data can support. The predictions can still be used, but this variance component should not be interpreted. The singularity lies in the species term, not in the site x species term that gives m4 its advantage. m2 and m3 share the same species term and are not flagged as singular, but in m3 the correlation is already 0.98, close to the boundary: the species intercepts and slopes are nearly collinear in every model. Here the choice is between m4, singular in a component that does not drive its predictions but clearly better in the cross-validation, and m3, a regular fit with a lower AUC. We keep m4 for the rest of the vignette and do not interpret its species correlation. Fitting m4 without the correlation (with (1 | species) + (0 + logit_conf | species)) would be a further option, but it is not one of the built-in candidates.

Calibration curves

plot_calibration() draws the calibrated probability against the score, one panel per species and one line per site. The points give the observed precision of the reviewed clips in 0.1-wide score bins, sized by the number of clips. The dashed line marks p_min.

plot_calibration(fit_full, val, p_min = 0.95, model_name = "m4_species_x_site")

Look for:

  • Flat or shallow curves. A species whose curve rises slowly, or never reaches p_min, is poorly separated from its false positives. Its calibrated detections should not enter the analyses, or only in a sensitivity analysis.
  • Sites that diverge. A site whose curve lies far from the others for the same species may differ in noise, in the number of false positives, or in the review. Check its clips before trusting its probabilities.
  • Curves that miss the points. Systematic departures from the observed precision indicate lack of fit, usually in the score bins with the largest points.
  • Few clips. Curves supported by small points (few clips per bin) are extrapolations. The "top" design gives few clips at low scores, so the lower part of each curve rests mainly on the shared fixed effects.

In the example, all of these appear. The three well-separated species (ela_bic, lep_pod, phy_cuv) have steep curves that cross p_min at moderate scores and lie close together among sites. pse_pla has a shallow curve that stays below p_min at every site: its false positives overlap its true detections too much for any score to be reliable. sci_nas and den_nan reach p_min only near the top of the score range, except at ARA, the quietest site, where their curves lie to the left. lep_fus diverges most among sites: its curves at ARA and BAI lie far below those at NHE and XAR. The species is rarely present at ARA and BAI, so most of its detections there are false, and these two cells also hold the fewest reviewed clips.

The practical consequence is the score at which each site x species reaches p_min. Under the global model this score is the same everywhere:

grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  species    = factor(levels(val$species), levels = levels(val$species)),
  site       = factor(levels(val$site), levels = levels(val$site)),
  confidence = seq(0.10, 0.99, by = 0.01)
) |>
  mutate(logit_conf = qlogis(confidence),
         p_global   = predict(fit_global, newdata = pick(everything()),
                              type = "response"),
         p_full     = predict(fit_full, newdata = pick(everything()),
                              type = "response"))

# lowest score with P(TP) >= 0.95; NA if never reached below 0.99
first_conf <- function(conf, p) {
  if (any(p >= 0.95)) min(conf[p >= 0.95]) else NA_real_
}
thresholds <- grid |>
  group_by(species, site) |>
  summarise(conf_global = first_conf(confidence, p_global),
            conf_full   = first_conf(confidence, p_full),
            .groups = "drop")
thresholds |> print(n = Inf)
#> # A tibble: 32 × 4
#>    species site  conf_global conf_full
#>    <fct>   <fct>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 boa_ran ARA           0.9      0.65
#>  2 boa_ran BAI           0.9      0.72
#>  3 boa_ran NHE           0.9      0.76
#>  4 boa_ran XAR           0.9      0.78
#>  5 den_nan ARA           0.9      0.8 
#>  6 den_nan BAI           0.9      0.95

#>  8 den_nan XAR           0.9      0.96
#>  9 ela_bic ARA           0.9      0.61
#> 10 ela_bic BAI           0.9      0.56
#> 11 ela_bic NHE           0.9      0.6 
#> 12 ela_bic XAR           0.9      0.58
#> 13 lep_fus ARA           0.9     NA   
#> 14 lep_fus BAI           0.9     NA   
#> 15 lep_fus NHE           0.9      0.91
#> 16 lep_fus XAR           0.9      0.91
#> 17 lep_pod ARA           0.9      0.61
#> 18 lep_pod BAI           0.9      0.65
#> 19 lep_pod NHE           0.9      0.7 
#> 20 lep_pod XAR           0.9      0.6 
#> 21 phy_cuv ARA           0.9      0.62
#> 22 phy_cuv BAI           0.9      0.63
#> 23 phy_cuv NHE           0.9      0.71
#> 24 phy_cuv XAR           0.9      0.69
#> 25 pse_pla ARA           0.9     NA

#> 29 sci_nas ARA           0.9      0.89
#> 30 sci_nas BAI           0.9      0.98
#> 31 sci_nas NHE           0.9      0.99
#> 32 sci_nas XAR           0.9      0.97

Under m4, the score needed to reach P(TP) >= 0.95 ranges from 0.56 to 0.99 among site x species combinations, and 6 combinations (lep_fus, pse_pla) never reach it, against a single threshold of 0.9 under the global model. A single score threshold, or a single calibration curve, would be too lenient for some species and sites and too strict for others.

Scoring every detection

score_detections() reads the complete selection tables (not only the reviewed clips) and predicts P(TP) for every detection of a calibrated species. The tables are passed as a vector named by site; the names must match the sites of the calibration. A site absent from the calibration is scored with the species effects only, with a warning. The night of a detection is its recording date, or the day before for recordings that start before dawn_hour.

sites  <- c("ARA", "XAR", "BAI", "NHE")
tables <- setNames(file.path(ex, "birdnet", sites,
                             "BirdNET_SelectionTable.txt"), sites)
scored <- score_detections(tables, fit_full, min_confidence = 0.1) |>
  suppressMessages()  # one line per site with the number of detections
scored |> select(site, species, night, confidence, p_tp)
#> # A tibble: 7,553 × 5
#>    site  species night    confidence   p_tp
#>    <chr> <fct>   <chr>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 ARA   boa_ran 20211001      0.504 0.734 
#>  2 ARA   den_nan 20211001      0.372 0.493 
#>  3 ARA   lep_fus 20211001      0.267 0.0173
#>  4 ARA   pse_pla 20211001      0.873 0.702 
#>  5 ARA   lep_pod 20211001      0.846 1.000 
#>  6 ARA   lep_pod 20211001      0.479 0.648 
#>  7 ARA   boa_ran 20211001      0.739 0.989 
#>  8 ARA   sci_nas 20211001      0.804 0.907 
#>  9 ARA   den_nan 20211001      0.240 0.267 
#> 10 ARA   sci_nas 20211001      0.623 0.785

Nightly detection histories

detection_history() aggregates the scored detections by site x species x night. A detection is reliable when its calibrated probability is at least p_min; the threshold applies to P(TP), not to the score. A night has a detection when it holds at least k reliable detections (min_detections_night, the repetition rule). The columns detection_k1 to detection_k3 give the same rule with k = 1, 2 and 3; detection uses the chosen k.

history <- detection_history(scored, p_min = 0.95, min_detections_night = 1)
history
#> # A tibble: 872 × 10
#>    site  species night    n_detections n_reliable p_tp_max detection_k1

#>  1 ARA   boa_ran 20211001           10          4    0.999            1

nights counts the nights with any scored detection, and nights_k1 to nights_k3 the nights with a detection under each rule. The gap between nights and nights_k1 is the number of nights whose detections were all below p_min: nights that a rule on the raw output (any detection above min_confidence) would have counted as detections. Species whose curves never reach p_min have no night with a detection, whatever their scores.

Choosing p_min and k

p_min and k trade false-positive nights against missed nights. A high p_min with k = 1 accepts a night on one very reliable detection; a lower p_min with k = 2 or 3 requires repeated, moderately reliable detections. The choice should follow the analysis: occupancy models with false-positive parameters can tolerate a lenient rule, whereas analyses with no false-positive component (for example, ordinations of community matrices) call for a strict one. The sensitivity of the number of nights with a detection to both settings is cheap to check:

sensitivity <- lapply(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99), function(p) {
  detection_history(scored, p_min = p) |>
    summarise(p_min = p, k1 = sum(detection_k1), k2 = sum(detection_k2),
              k3 = sum(detection_k3))
}) |>
  bind_rows()
sensitivity
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   p_min    k1    k2    k3
#>   <dbl> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1  0.8    460   400   360
#> 2  0.9    394   351   318
#> 3  0.95   358   323   294
#> 4  0.99   315   288   258

The number of nights with a detection under k = 1 falls from 460 to 315 across this range of p_min. If the conclusions of the downstream analysis change across the range, report the results under more than one setting.

The same check applies to the choice of model. Scoring with the global model and comparing the histories shows how many site x species x nights change, and for which species:

history_global <- score_detections(tables, fit_global) |>
  suppressMessages() |>
  detection_history(p_min = 0.95)
compare <- inner_join(history, history_global,
                      by = c("site", "species", "night"),
                      suffix = c("_full", "_global"))
compare_sp <- compare |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(nights = n(),
            k1_full = sum(detection_k1_full),
            k1_global = sum(detection_k1_global),
            differ_k1 = sum(detection_k1_full != detection_k1_global))
compare_sp
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   species nights k1_full k1_global differ_k1
#>   <fct>    <int>   <int>     <int>     <int>
#> 1 boa_ran    115      68        50        18
#> 2 den_nan    118      30        22        22
#> 3 ela_bic    101      85        65        20
#> 4 lep_fus    103       3         4         1
#> 5 lep_pod     96      78        66        12
#> 6 phy_cuv    103      81        66        15
#> 7 pse_pla    118       0        21        21
#> 8 sci_nas    118      13        29        18

The global model changes the history of 127 of 872 site x species x nights under k = 1. It accepts fewer nights than m4 for boa_ran, den_nan, ela_bic, lep_pod, phy_cuv, which reach P(TP) >= 0.95 below the common threshold at some or all sites, and more nights for lep_fus, pse_pla, sci_nas, whose calibrated probabilities m4 places lower.

When the global model is enough

The global model is enough when the hierarchical models do not improve the cross-validated AUC beyond the fold-to-fold variation, when the species and site curves of a hierarchical model lie close together near p_min, and when the detection histories do not change between models. None of these holds in the example. With very few species or sites the variance components are poorly estimated, and a simpler model (a species effect only, or the global model) is the more defensible choice; with many species, or species and sites known to differ in noise, the hierarchical models keep the threshold on P(TP) consistent across them.

Model checks

Before using calibrated probabilities, check that:

  1. The GLMM converged. fit_calibration() warns when the refitted model is singular, as it did for m4 above, and convergence warnings of lme4::glmer() are passed on. compare_calibration_models() drops a fold whose fit fails from the mean AUC, warns about it and counts it in n_failed. Inspect the refitted model directly:

    lme4::isSingular(fit_full)
#> [1] TRUE
fit_full@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages
#> [1] "boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')"

    Here the only message is the singular fit discussed above; there are no convergence warnings. Convergence warnings (as opposed to a singular fit) mean the estimates should not be used: simplify the random-effect structure, or review more clips.

  2. The cross-validation supports the choice. Read auc_sd with auc_mean. Do not prefer a more complex model on a difference smaller than the fold-to-fold variation.

  3. The calibration curves are sensible. Curves should increase with the score, follow the observed precision, and rest on enough clips near p_min. calibration_effort() estimates how many clips per site x species are needed for a stable AUC.

The calibration also assumes that, within a score level, the reviewed clips are representative of all the detections of that species at that site. The model is conditional on the score, so the "top" design, which oversamples high scores, does not bias it as long as this holds. It fails if the clips were chosen by another criterion related to correctness (for example, only clips that sounded clear, or only the nights of peak activity), or if the reviewed period differs from the scored one in noise or in species composition.

One species, or one site

When models is omitted, compare_calibration_models() chooses the family from the observed levels. For one species at several sites it compares a global model, a site intercept and a site intercept/slope model. The same choice is automatic in calibrate(). One species at one site needs only the global model; multiple species at one site use the species-effect candidates without non-estimable site random effects. Unused factor levels do not count as observed species or sites.

To construct the single-species family explicitly, use calibration_models(single_species = TRUE). An explicit list overrides automatic choice in the comparison. The original multispecies family and its ordering remain available through calibration_models().

The performance vignette documents the Curiango regression checks and the multispecies simulation; it distinguishes predictive performance from changes in detection histories.

Keeping recordings and nights intact

fold_group = "source_audio" keeps recordings together, and fold_group = "night" keeps nights together. The group key always includes site and spans all species: detections of the same recording or night cannot leak across training and test sets through different species. Group counts are balanced within site; clip counts may differ. Each site needs at least k_folds distinct groups. This evaluates new recordings or nights at known sites, not transfer to new sites. Rare species may be absent from a particular train or test partition.

Retain the metadata explicitly when assembling the stages by hand:

val_grouped <- read_validations(val_files, keep = c("source_audio", "night"))
folds <- calibration_folds(val_grouped, k_folds = 5, seed = 2026,
                           fold_group = "night")
cv_grouped <- compare_calibration_models(
  val_grouped, models, k_folds = 5, seed = 2026, fold_group = "night")
selected <- select_calibration_model(cv_grouped, k_folds = 5)

For custom tables, a vector of column names can define a compound group, e.g. fold_group = c("recorder", "night"). IDs must be nonempty and nonmissing. Supply real recording/night metadata; grouping by clip file, species or verdict would not preserve the acoustic unit.

calibrate(fold_group = "night", ...) retains the requested input columns automatically and saves the assignments in calibration_folds.csv for inspection. Older validation tables without those columns still work with the default clip folds. Asking for absent metadata raises an error. A test fold containing only one verdict has undefined AUC; log-loss and Brier remain available, and it is not counted as a failed fit. AUC-based selection requires at least one finite AUC.

The calibrate() wrapper

calibrate() runs the whole stage in one call. It reads the clips, compares the candidate models, refits the one chosen by the rule in select, plots the calibration curves (if ggplot2 is installed), scores every detection, builds the detection history and writes all the outputs to output_dir. The default select = "one_se_logloss" applies the log-loss and one-standard-error rule described above. Set select = "best_auc" to retain the 2.x selection by highest mean AUC; that rule can retain a singular model and warns on a singular final fit. Use uncorrelated = TRUE to include the uncorrelated m4 variant in the candidates. Read the comparison, calibration_model.txt and the curves before using the output.

out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "calibration")
res <- calibrate(validation_files  = val_files,
                 prediction_tables = tables,
                 output_dir        = out_dir,
                 select = "one_se_logloss", uncorrelated = TRUE,
                 p_min = 0.95, min_detections_night = 1, k_folds = 5) |>
  suppressMessages()
deparse1(res$fit@call$formula)  # the model calibrate() refitted
#> [1] "tp ~ logit_conf + (1 | species) + (0 + logit_conf | species) + (1 | site:species)"
list.files(out_dir)
#>  [1] "calibrated_detections_ARA.csv" "calibrated_detections_BAI.csv"
#>  [3] "calibrated_detections_NHE.csv" "calibrated_detections_XAR.csv"
#>  [5] "calibration_curves.png"        "calibration_model.rds"        
#>  [7] "calibration_model.txt"         "detection_summary.csv"        
#>  [9] "model_comparison.csv"          "nightly_detection_history.csv"

nightly_detection_history.csv is the input of the occupancy and community analyses (see vignette("frognet-workflow")). Five folds and the example’s 2467 clips run in seconds; a project with thousands of clips and many species takes longer, and effort_curve = TRUE adds the effort curve.
